rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2014> the study reports its own 2018 season data from one soybean field in Arkansas: five UAV RGB acquisitions, four EMI soil ECa surveys, in-situ soil sensors, 12 soil samples, 31 ground plots and combine-harvester yield point data; Table 1, Fig. 5, Tables 2-3 report its own classification accuracy, UAV-vs-ground validation and correlations.
rows.notes: The study uses UAV RGB imagery (plus EMI geophysics) to map plant spatial abundance, vigor (GCC) and height and identifies persistent anomalous areas of low plant development; these anomalies are attributed to soil clay content (high ECa) and to a soil-moisture decline linked to non-uniform furrow irrigation controlled by topography, and are correlated with yield (Table 3). It does not detect pests, diseases or nutrient deficiencies, the abnormalities named in the passage, and it tests no intervention or production gain following detection; the link from detection to maximized production is only asserted. Detection of soil-driven anomalies is at most a precondition of the claimed crop-production effect, so Q2 is answered no and upstream set to true.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2014> own field data (UAV time-series, EMI surveys, soil sensors, soil samples, ground plots, yield map) from a soybean field in Arkansas, 2018 season.
rows.notes: The study applies a machine-learning (SVM with attribute profiles) classification of UAV imagery to identify anomalous low-productivity zones, but it contains no IoT-connected sprayers, no targeted fertilizer or pesticide application, no measurement of chemical use and no test of enhanced crop health following targeted application. It only maps anomalies and correlates them with soil properties and yield; the zone identification is a precondition of the claimed targeted-application effect, so Q2 is no and upstream is true.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2014> own field data (UAV time-series, EMI surveys, soil sensors, soil samples, ground plots, yield map) from a soybean field in Arkansas, 2018 season.
rows.notes: The study does not address pests at all: the anomalous zones it identifies from UAV imagery are attributed to soil clay content and soil-moisture/irrigation non-uniformity, not pest infestation, and no pesticide application, pest-control outcome or chemical-use reduction is reported. At most it shows that UAV imagery can delineate affected zones, a precondition of the claimed targeted pest control, so Q2 is no and upstream is true.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Single field, single season (2018), soybean only; study integrates UAV RGB products with EMI soil ECa and yield data. None of the three claims (pest/disease/nutrient detection; IoT sprayer targeted application; pest control) is tested by the study, which concerns soil heterogeneity and irrigation-related soil moisture as controls on plant development and yield.
